extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners: attorneys, patent examiners, applicants, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing withdrawal, substitution, continuations, abandonment, allowance, forfeiture/renewal, delivery, and interference procedures for patent applications — including how dates, priority, and legal effect are determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned application has no legal existence
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned application has no legal existence or validity for any purpose; it cannot aid a subsequent application by carrying back the date of application, nor is it further noticed by the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases (e.g., Ex parte Casilear). An abandoned application is not treated as prior art aid to later filings and is not noticed except in limited circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and substitution of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time before final rejection or allowance an application may be withdrawn by the applicant and a new application filed with a new specification, oath, drawing, and fee; after final rejection a new one may be filed though the rejected application cannot then be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the new application is a continuation/substitute of the old depends on abandonment; relation rests on abandonment facts. Cases cited in §580 illustrate limits (e.g., Ex parte Golding, Sexton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation of all claims is abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: The cancellation of all the claims in an application is an abandonment of the application/invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific authority cited (Lasscell). Cancellation that leaves no claims is effectively an abandonment to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary worthlessness of invention does not excuse delay
rubrics_metrics.description: That the present pecuniary worthlessness of an invention does not excuse delay in prosecuting the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay caused by belief that invention is not yet valuable is not an acceptable excuse for failing to prosecute; cited Ex parte Woodbridge and other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a second application is not necessarily withdrawal of the first
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of a second application is not necessarily a withdrawal of the first application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the first is abandoned depends on facts; a second application that merely describes an improvement without claiming it does not abandon the improvement claimed in the former application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned application cannot be revived
rubrics_metrics.description: An application once abandoned can never be revived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited (Ex parte Mayor, Marsh v. Sayles). Once final abandonment occurs, revival is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuations/substituted applications relate back to original if not abandoned and filed without unreasonable delay (two-year rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If original applications were not abandoned, and new ones have been filed without unreasonable delay and within the two years limited by law, they are regarded as substitutes/continuations and on questions of novelty and abandonment their dates relate back to the dates of the originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the new application is a true continuation filed within statutory limits and without unreasonable delay, public uses/subsequent events are measured from the original filing date. See §580 and related cases (e.g., Graham v. McCormick).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether two applications are continuous is a question of fact to be decided by the circumstances of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trier considers whether the inventor intended to abandon the original by his acts, lapse of time, conduct (e.g., patenting other things), attorney delays, and whether the invention was abandoned to the public. Many cases illustrate fact-specific inquiries (Weston v. White, Bevin v. East Hampton Bell Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapse of time is strong evidence of abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: The lapse of time between applications is of great weight, if not conclusive, in determining abandonment of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples: delays of 8, 10, 15, 18 years have been treated as abandonment in cited cases (Consolidated Fruit Jar Co. v. Bellaire Stamping Co., Marsh v. Commissioner, Bevin v. East Hampton Bell Co.). Context and reason for delay matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second application for part of an invention disclosed in a pending application is a continuation as to two-years' public use
rubrics_metrics.description: When a second application is made for part of an invention disclosed in a former and still-pending application, the later is a continuation of the former insofar as the two-years' public-use question is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Graham v. McCormick and related decisions; partial claiming can preserve the earlier date for specific issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituted applications are continuations and bear the original date
rubrics_metrics.description: It is immaterial how many substituted applications are filed; substituted applications are continuations of the original and the patent, when granted, will rest on the original application as represented in its successors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §581: the number or duration of successor filings does not change that the patent rests on the original unless legislative change or abandonment intervenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of allowance and six‑month final fee payment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner or board decides the applicant is entitled to a patent, notice of allowance is sent calling for payment of the final fee within six months; if fee is paid within that period the patent is prepared for issue. Until such notice the patent is not 'allowed' within the law and the case remains under examiner control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six-month period does not begin until notice of allowance is given (§582). If allowance is withdrawn and later allowed again, a new notice is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: After allowance, withdrawal from issue requires Commissioner approval; after final fee paid, limited grounds to withhold or withdraw
rubrics_metrics.description: After allowance the case will not be withdrawn from issue except upon approval of the Commissioner; after the final fee has been paid and the case has received its date and number, it cannot be withdrawn except for mistake by the Office, fraud or illegality in the application, or interference proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application is regarded as pending until letters-patent are delivered; minor administrative acts (file wrapper signature) matter for control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance is not binding on the Commissioner until letters-patent issued; Commissioner may withhold patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The allowance of an application by the examiner or board does not oblige the Commissioner to grant the patent; the Commissioner may withhold issuance if in his judgment the invention is not patentable, issuance is forbidden by statute, or the patent would probably be held invalid by courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner should not withhold issuance unnecessarily; withholding is a discretionary power and may be exercised in extreme cases (Ex parte Neale, Smith v. Perry).

rubrics_metrics.name: File-wrapper signature and control until seal affixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Until the file-wrapper is signed and the application forwarded to the Issue Division the case is still under the examiner's control; until the seal is affixed the patent is not complete and the Commissioner may in extreme cases withhold the seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affixing the seal gives finality; withholding the seal should be rare and limited to clear violations (manifestly old claims, fraud, illegality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandamus to compel issuance limited where discretion exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A writ of mandamus to direct the Commissioner to award a patent will not lie to compel acts which the law leaves to his discretion; mandamus, when granted, is conclusive only on the Patent Office and the public, not on other claimants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandamus is available only where duty is ministerial rather than discretionary. Cases: United States v. Butterworth, Hull v. Commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to pay final fee forfeits application; renewal within two years allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to pay the final fee within six months after notice of allowance forfeits the application and no patent can be issued. However, within two years after notice of allowance any interested person may file a new application for the same invention using original materials and paying a new fee; this second application is not a continuation and bears date from the renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal is examined like an original application; novelty is determined by the state of the art when the original was filed, and abandonment is a question of fact. Forfeiture is generally incurable after two years except under narrow case law exceptions (Ex parte Barnitz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal applications treated as new originals except limited relation back
rubrics_metrics.description: A renewal application filed after forfeiture stands on its own date and is examined as an original application; in some cases a renewal within two years may be treated as a continuation for certain purposes (e.g., under Sec. 4897) and relate back to the prior application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee may renew after forfeiture; ratification of unauthorized attorney acts in renewing may be void as to intervening rights; specific cases (Thomson v. Waterhouse, Weir v. Morden) illustrate nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeited applications remain secret and are not cited as references
rubrics_metrics.description: While an application remains forfeited no notice is given to the applicant of subsequent applications, and forfeited or abandoned applications are not cited as references to defeat later applicants; they remain in the Patent Office's secret archives and are open only to the applicant or his attorney except by order of the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeited applications are treated as 'dead' for public reference purposes (Opinion Acting-Commissioner 1877). Copies may be released only by special order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final fee payment methods and delivery of patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The final fee may be paid to the Commissioner, the Treasurer, assistant treasurers, designated depositaries, national banks, or receivers of public money; the patent will be delivered or mailed on the day of its date to the patentee or to the attorney of record if one exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without specific request the Office will not deliver the patent to an associate or substitute attorney; prescribed payment channels must be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference proceedings determine priority of invention (first-to-invent with due diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference is instituted to determine the priority between rival inventors who claim substantially the same patentable invention; the law awards a single patent to the party who first conceived the invention and reduced it to practice, provided he used due diligence in reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference procedure is the contested proceeding for deciding priority (see §586). It is declared between applications (not merely applicants) and focuses on which invention was first produced; title issues may remain separate from the interference outcome (Hibbard v. Richmond and historical notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference declared between applications rather than applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference is declared between applications (and patents) rather than directly between applicants; it is intended to find which invention was first produced, not solely who has title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of title can appear separate from statutory priority questions; interference machinery (per §4904) is designed to adjudicate priority facts with evidentiary hearings.
